By Gu Ting for RFA Mandarin 2023.11.07 -- A Chinese court yesterday handed down a harsh ten-year jail term to a former state-owned enterprise employee for handing sensitive 'corporate intelligence' to foreign agents. The Chengdu Intermediate People's Court in Sichuan sentenced Wang to ten years' imprisonment and confiscated 2 million yuan (US$272,400) of his assets after convicting him of 'espionage,' state media reported. Wang once led the overseas branch of a major state-owned company, now central to a high-profile China spying case spanning over a decade. His name appeared in 20 critical documents submitted as evidence, all deemed 'state secrets' under China's recently expanded legal definitions. A Chinese lawyer, who wished to remain anonymous, warned that the amended Counter-Espionage Law now classifies even publicly available information as 'state secrets,' leaving ordinary citizens and businesses vulnerable to prosecution. 'It's absurd,' the lawyer said. 'Information freely available online is now treated as classified, turning everyday business activities into potential espionage.' The law's changes have sparked widespread fear, as authorities can now access corporate facilities and digital devices without warrants, targeting even routine market research as espionage. Journalists, activists, and lawyers are at particular risk, with many facing imprisonment for sharing already published information. Political journalist Gao Yu, who served time for leaking 'state secrets' that were publicly accessible, warns of a surge in such cases under the new law. 'This isn't just about officials,' she said. 'Ordinary people in business, trade, and media are now at risk.' Wang's case signals a chilling new era of surveillance and control, as China intensifies its crackdown on perceived threats amid rising global tensions.
